title: The Risalah
hook: his book laid out the method of law, founding usul al-fiqh

segments.voice: Yesterday, Imam al-Shafi'i, and your line: learned from both. When two people you respect disagreed, what was each of them right about? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

It begins as a letter. A hadith scholar in Basra, Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi, writes to al-Shafi'i with a request, as the story is told: write me something on how the Qur'an is to be understood, on when a report is to be accepted, on consensus, and on how one text can replace another. Explain how it all fits. Al-Shafi'i answers, and the answer grows into a book. It keeps the plain name of what it was: al-Risalah, the letter. With it, scholars had a shared page on which to argue over method, not only over rulings. Today: the Risalah.
screen: `A REQUEST FROM BASRA.` → `HOW DOES IT ALL FIT?` → `THE ANSWER BECOMES A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Start with the question underneath it. These last two weeks we've seen Kufa's careful judgment and Medina's living practice, each strong, each sure of itself. Al-Shafi'i asked something prior: before any ruling, how do we know where to look, and in what order? That's usul al-fiqh, the roots of law, and tradition remembers the Risalah as the book where that discipline begins. Next, the order he set. The Qur'an first. Then the sunnah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, which al-Shafi'i argued explains the Qur'an and must be followed, even when it comes through a single reliable narrator. That point pushed against Medina's practice, where the city could outweigh a lone report. Then consensus. Then analogy, qiyas, measured carefully from a text. Then a method for language. A verse can sound general and still be meant more narrowly. One text can explain another. When two reports seem to clash, al-Shafi'i's first move is to look for a way both are true before setting either aside. Last, the argument we met with Abu Hanifa's school. In the Risalah he rejects juristic preference, istihsan, where it isn't tied to a text, calling it a jurist pleasing himself. The Hanafis kept arguing back. Some readers say that even then, the argument ran in his terms: what is your source, and what is your step? That's the index line in two words. Not the answer first. Method first.
screen: `USUL AL-FIQH: THE ROOTS OF LAW.` · `QUR'AN, SUNNAH, CONSENSUS, ANALOGY.` · `TWO REPORTS CLASH: SEEK BOTH TRUE.` · `WHAT IS YOUR SOURCE, YOUR STEP?`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one principle of method. Here's one al-Shafi'i works through: a text that sounds general can be explained by another that's more specific. The Qur'an gives children shares in their parents' estate, in general terms. A report in Jami' al-Tirmidhi says a killer does not inherit. The general rule stands; the specific one narrows it. Now try it on your own life. Take a broad rule you keep, like always answering your phone for family. Is there a specific exception you already live by? Name it. Notice how the two fit together instead of fighting. If you pray, you can ask for clear understanding. The bell holds the time.
The Risalah. Al-Shafi'i's letter that grew into a book, setting out how law is to be found: its sources, their order, and how texts explain each other. Today's word.
Your line: method first. Today, before you argue about an answer, ask the other person how they got there, and tell them how you got to yours. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Students of Islamic law study usul al-fiqh, the roots of law, alongside the rulings themselves, and al-Shafi'i's Risalah is read as a foundational work in that field.

pairs: a specific text narrows a general one

al-Shafi'i argued that a reliable report from a single narrator must be followed

fork.setup: you're al-Shafi'i. two sound reports seem to say opposite things. what's your first move?
options: pick the one that suits the case.
set both aside and use your own judgment.
look for a way both can be true.
fork.reveal: reconcile first. only if that fails does he ask whether one replaced the other, or weigh them.

original.note: Arabic: the letter, the message; the name of al-Shafi'i's book on method.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Risalah is a book of rulings.
what it means: it's a book about how to reach rulings: which sources, in what order, and how texts explain each other.
what a scholar hears: usul al-fiqh, khabar al-wahid as binding, 'amm and khass, and al-Shafi'i's rejection of istihsan.

notes: The request from Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi and its contents: told as 'as the story is told'; confirm.
Index says 'founding usul al-fiqh'; the script says 'tradition remembers the Risalah as the book where that discipline begins'. Confirm framing.
The order of sources and the single-report argument as set out in the Risalah; the contrast with Medinan practice: confirm fairness.
Reconcile-first approach to conflicting reports (then abrogation, then weighing): confirm as al-Shafi'i's method.
Al-Shafi'i on istihsan as a jurist pleasing himself (taladhdhudh): confirm it is in the Risalah (also Ibtal al-Istihsan in al-Umm).

Qur'an 4:11 (children's shares) paraphrased, and Tirmidhi 2109 (the killer does not inherit) as an example of the specific narrowing the general: confirm number and that al-Shafi'i uses this kind of example.
